content: Dr. Luz Maria De-Regil was granted full participation in discussions and decision-making regarding recommendations for the project spanning 2007 to 2010. She disclosed that her current employer is an international non-governmental organization focused on improving micronutrient status among infants, children, and women, primarily funded by the Canadian government. This organization, the Micronutrient Initiative, is dedicated to addressing vitamin and mineral deficiencies in vulnerable populations, including efforts related to multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs). Dr. De-Regil also declared her co-authorship of systematic reviews on the following topics: (a) point-of-use fortification of foods with MNPs containing iron for preschool and school-aged children, (b) MNPs for point-of-use fortification in pregnant women, and (c) point-of-use fortification with MNPs for health and nutrition in children under two years of age. Additionally, she contributed to the preparation of WHO guidelines on point-of-use fortification with MNPs as a former WHO staff member. While she participated in deliberations as a member of the guideline development group, she recused herself from voting on the recommendations. Dr. Rukhsana Haider, employed by the Training and Assistance for Health and Nutrition Foundation in Dhaka, Bangladesh, disclosed her membership in the Technical Advisory Group for Helen Keller International’s ARCH (Assessment and Research on Child Feeding) Project at the time of the meeting. She was allowed full participation in discussions and decision-making on the recommendations. Dr. Maria Elena del Socorro Jefferds, employed by the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), declared her role as a co-investigator in a CDC-funded study on the effectiveness of MNPs in Kenya. She is the lead author and co-author of several publications on this topic, including a special Sight and Life supplement on MNPs published in 2013. She also participated in a UNICEF/CDC workshop on scaling up MNP interventions for infants and young children aged 6–23 months. Furthermore, she coordinated and authored a monitoring manual for home fortification interventions, including MNPs, for the Home Fortification Technical Advisory Group. Dr. Jefferds was an investigator in the first global assessment of home fortification interventions and the lead author of the corresponding report and related journal article, both published in 2013. She is also a co-author of a Cochrane systematic review on MNP interventions in infants and children aged 6–23 months and 2–12 years. While she participated in deliberations on recommendations related to MNPs, she recused herself from voting on recommendations concerning the use of MNPs for point-of-use fortification of foods. Dr. Lynnette Neufeld disclosed that her current employer had received funding in the past four years for research and programming related to MNPs, although she is not leading any of these initiatives. In her previous position with a different employer, she was involved in research studies related to MNPs. She also declared her membership on the Steering Committee of the Home Fortification Technical Advisory Group. Dr. Neufeld participated in deliberations on recommendations related to MNPs but recused herself from voting on recommendations concerning the use of MNPs for point-of-use fortification of foods. All other members of the guideline development group completed and signed written declarations of interest before the meeting and made verbal declarations during the meeting. These interests were deemed not relevant to the guideline on the use of MNPs for point-of-use fortification of foods consumed by infants and young children aged 6–23 months and children aged 2–12 years. External experts also declared their interests but did not participate in the deliberations or decision-making process. The WHO Secretariat will continue to monitor research developments in the field of micronutrient interventions targeting infants and young children aged 6–23 months and children aged 2–12 years. If the guideline requires an update or if concerns arise regarding its validity, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development will coordinate the update following the formal procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development.
